haiku-low.q1: MySQL commits first with an outbox row, then a guarded copy goes to Postgres (500 ms timeout). Postgres errors are logged and counted; the request succeeds.
haiku-low.q2: Only when the stored row's version is lower than the incoming version, and no tombstone exists for the id.
haiku-low.q3: Every deployed instance must report users_dual_write on, all reporting, then a further 60 s wait. Instances can disagree for up to 30 s.
haiku-low.q4: Reads the replica in batches of 2000, pausing while replica lag exceeds 5 s. Only one worker runs, holding a 60 s lease.
haiku-low.q5: Reads: a clean verifier pass after backfill, then ramp to 100%. Source: 72 h at 100% reads, a recent clean pass, low outbox, healthy Postgres, operator approval.
haiku-low.q6: Outbox row in MySQL's users_outbox, same transaction as the write. The repairer copies the current row to Postgres, then deletes the outbox row.
haiku-low.q7: Copies lock it and skip if a tombstone exists. Erase takes the same lock and atomically writes a tombstone and deletes the row.
haiku-low.q8: backfill_last_id in MySQL users_migration_state, updated after each Postgres batch commits; a crash re-copies safely. Stops on empty batch or lost lease.
haiku-low.q9: The verifier merge-walks both tables by id. Mismatches get rechecked on the primary, then queued for repair via outbox; tombstoned Postgres rows get removed.
haiku-low.q10: Writes check the control row (source, pause, epoch); step 5 fences the old source. Drains over 45 s abort before step 4; later, roll forward.
haiku-low.q11: Each switch sets the new source's id sequence above the largest id in either store plus 1,000,000. Rollback verifies MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT exceeds the largest id.
haiku-low.q12: Mirrored to MySQL via the Postgres outbox. Rollback: procedure S to MySQL, once backlog drains. Ends at step 11, when mirror is off.

sonnet.q1: MySQL first: one MySQL transaction (control check, write, read back, outbox row) commits, then the guarded copy to Postgres runs (500 ms timeout). If Postgres fails, the error is caught, logged and counted; the request still succeeds and the repairer handles it.
sonnet.q2: Only if the stored version is lower than the incoming version (and no tombstone exists for the id). If the stored version is equal or higher, the row is left alone.
sonnet.q3: Every deployed instance must report users_dual_write = on (reporting count equals deployed count; old builds not exporting the metric count as not ready), then wait a further 60 s. Instances can disagree on a flag for up to 30 s.
sonnet.q4: Backfill reads from the replica, not the primary, in batches of 2000 ordered by id. It checks mysql_replica_lag_seconds before each batch and, if lag is above 5 s, sleeps 1 s and rechecks without reading rows. It runs in a dedicated single worker holding a lease. (The only primary write is updating backfill_last_id.)
sonnet.q5: Reads to Postgres: step 4 backfill is complete and last_clean_pass_at is set (a clean verifier pass after backfill completed); then ramp 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%. Source switch: 72 h at 100% Postgres reads (read_100_since), clean pass less than 24 h old with no open mismatches, outbox count below threshold and oldest row under 60 s, Postgres healthy, replica lag normal, no backfill lease held, and operator approval.
sonnet.q6: The outbox row (holding the user id), written in the same MySQL transaction as the write, records it. It is kept in the MySQL source database (users_outbox). The repairer reads the current row from the source primary and runs the guarded copy to Postgres, then deletes the outbox row.
sonnet.q7: Tombstones: erase writes a permanent tombstone (id only) and deletes the row in one transaction. Every guarded copy takes the lock on the id and skips the copy if a tombstone exists, so backfill and repair cannot re-create the user.
sonnet.q8: Progress is backfill_last_id (plus the lease) in users_migration_state on the MySQL primary, set after each batch's Postgres transaction. A crash between copy and update just re-reads and re-copies the batch, which is safe because the guarded copy is idempotent. It stops when a batch read returns empty, marking backfill complete (or if it loses its lease).
sonnet.q9: The verifier. It merge-joins both tables in primary-key order, comparing id, email, name, plan, version, updated_at, and also finds Postgres rows with no MySQL row. Each mismatched id is rechecked after its outbox rows are gone against the MySQL primary; if still different, it inserts an outbox row and the repairer fixes it automatically. A tombstoned id found in Postgres is removed. Repeating mismatches block the next gate.
sonnet.q10: Procedure S uses control rows (not flags) with shared locks: pause the old source (exclusive lock waits for in-flight writes), drain outbox, commit point in new source with epoch+1, fence old source (refuses writes with 503), then unpause. Every write checks its own store's control row for source, write_paused = 0 and matching cached epoch, so stale instances are refused. If it runs long: drain limit is 45 s; before step 4 it aborts by unpausing the old source with nothing changed; after step 4 it always rolls forward. The pause budget is about 50 s within the 90 s limit.
sonnet.q11: Postgres assigns ids (GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY, which also accepts explicit ids). Each time the source changes, the new source's sequence is set above the largest id seen in either store plus 1,000,000; on rollback to MySQL, its AUTO_INCREMENT is set likewise and checked to be above the largest id before unpausing.
sonnet.q12: While Postgres is the source, writes go to Postgres with an outbox row there, then a guarded copy into MySQL; the repairer mirrors Postgres outbox rows to MySQL and the verifier keeps comparing. Rollback is procedure S with Postgres as old source and MySQL as new (gates: mirror backlog drained or drainable, clean pass after step 8 and under 24 h old, MySQL reachable; set users_read_source to MySQL first; check AUTO_INCREMENT before unpausing). Only possible during step 9 (at least 14 days); it ends at step 11, when mirror = off and MySQL stops receiving writes.
